comparedAgainst: https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/23quicksort/ (cited source, also a ranking page for this query)
justification: Target queries 'quicksort worst case' and 'big o average case'. Pages read: Wikipedia's Quicksort article (defines best/average/worst with the ~1.39 n log2 n constant and McIlroy's AntiQuicksort, but no security angle, no .NET/C#, nothing run); Wikipedia's 'Best, worst and average case' article (general definitions across several structures, no randomized-algorithm treatment, no expected-case-vs-average-case distinction, no algorithmic-complexity-attack material); GeeksforGeeks' Quick Sort page (states the three complexities with no probabilistic derivation, mentions random-pivot as 'preferred' with no proof of why, no duplicate-key/three-way partitioning, no hash-flooding, no measured output, only a static input/output example). Against all three this article has clear original value: it derives the average case from first principles with the standard indicator-variable argument (attributed to CLRS/Sedgewick and Wayne as the standard assumption, not presented as an original theorem), it measures real comparison counts and recursion depths on this machine for sorted/reversed/duplicate/random inputs across two working programs plus two exercises, it reproduces an actual CVE (MS11-100 / CVE-2011-3414) and the Crosby-Wallach algorithmic-complexity-attack paper as a second real-world instance of the same 'deterministic scheme, adversary who knows it' pattern, and it explains why .NET's per-process randomized string hash defeats that specific attack, none of which appears in any of the three compared pages. It cleanly distinguishes best/average/worst/expected case with a closing table, which none of the three compared pages does as precisely. Quote audit (the session's most common finding, checked line by line): re-fetched all eight front-matter sources. StackOverflowException docs -- 'is thrown when the execution stack exceeds the stack size' and 'you can't catch a StackOverflowException object with a try/catch block, and the corresponding process is terminated by default' -- both verbatim. String.GetHashCode docs -- 'the hash code itself is not guaranteed to be stable', 'two subsequent runs of the same program may return different hash codes', 'should never be persisted' -- all verbatim. Microsoft Security Advisory 2659883 -- title 'Vulnerability in ASP.NET Could Allow Denial of Service', CVE-2011-3414, 'Collisions in HashTable May Cause DoS Vulnerability', MS11-100, December 2011 -- all verbatim/accurate. dotnet/runtime Marvin.cs -- DefaultSeed is a static property generated once via the OS's cryptographic RNG (Interop.GetRandomBytes / RandomNumberGenerator), matching the article's 'a 64-bit value drawn once per process from the operating system's cryptographic random number generator'. dotnet/runtime String.Comparison.cs -- the GetNonRandomizedHashCode comment 'Use if and only if "Denial of Service" attacks are not a concern (i.e. never used for free-form user input), or are otherwise mitigated' is verbatim, and the parameterless GetHashCode() does call Marvin.ComputeHash32 seeded from Marvin.DefaultSeed as described. Sedgewick and Wayne (algs4.cs.princeton.edu) -- '~2 N ln N compares... on the average', the lightning-probability sentence, and the duplicate-keys 'might seem to create unnecessary exchanges... crucial to avoiding quadratic running time in certain typical applications' are all verbatim. Crosby and Wallach (USENIX Security 2003) -- 'both binary trees and hash tables can degenerate to linked lists with carefully chosen input' is verbatim (checked against two independent fetches of the paper). No fabricated or altered quote found anywhere on the page. Citation completeness: all eight front-matter sources are cited inline at the point of the claim they support (CLRS ch. 7 for the average-case derivation and worst-case recurrence; Sedgewick and Wayne for the constant, the lightning line, and duplicate-key handling; Crosby/Wallach for the attack; the Microsoft advisory for the CVE; String.GetHashCode, StackOverflowException, Marvin.cs and String.Comparison.cs each for their specific claim). No listed-but-uncited source, which was this session's other established pilot-round lesson. Structure and filler: first sentence delivers a specific, checkable claim (the first-element pivot's reproducible failure mode), no restated title, no 'in this article' framing, no conclusion-that-says-nothing; the closing section states the honest, scoped summary table rather than a boilerplate wrap-up. Exercises are placed through the body (after the recurrences, after the average-case derivation, after the duplicate-keys section, after the hash-flooding callout, and at the very end) rather than stacked under a single terminal 'Exercises' heading -- the pilot-round ending-template lesson does not apply here. Predict-the-output items (the Dictionary lookup exercise) keep their output panel inside the collapsed solution, not exposed above the question. The toolchain sentence ('.NET 10 (SDK 10.0.401, runtime 10.0.12) on Windows 11, x64') sits in prose immediately after the first output block, consistent with the placement this session has held every other AdSense-passing article to (amortized-analysis, big-o-notation, how-git-works, relational-model-and-keys, test-driven-development) -- not a stamped opener. No ad code, no keyword stuffing; title and description read for a human and match the content. docs/crosslinks/complexity/best-average-worst-case.md exists, lists sensible pending links with location and rationale, and includes a boundaries section against near-duplicate coverage with the planned hash-tables, sorting-comparison and recursion-analysis articles, so the missing-sibling-link problem does not apply. run-code.mjs: PASS, blocks=17, executed=6. Why 8.7 and not higher: two real but narrow issues, below.

issues.location: 'Extend the code: fix the duplicates case' exercise solution, id=ex-threeway, `QuicksortThreeWay`/inner while loop
issues.problem: The three-way partition code keeps Sedgewick and Wayne's own variable names for two of the three pointers (`lt`, `gt` -- identical to their published Quick3way.java) and their exact three-branch structure (scan-and-swap-into-lt, scan-and-swap-into-gt, else advance), only renaming the scanning index from `i` to `k` and translating exch() calls to C# tuple swaps. The prose above it is honest about the source ('Sedgewick and Wayne's three-way scheme'), which is the right instinct, but hard rule 4 asks for the team's own variable names even when the algorithm and its attribution are not in question, and `lt`/`gt` is a distinctive enough naming choice (not a generic `lo`/`hi`/`i`/`j`) that it reads as transcribed rather than reimplemented from understanding.
issues.fixLooksLike: Rename the two carried-over pointers to something that is not Sedgewick and Wayne's own naming, e.g. `belowPivot`/`abovePivot` or `lowBoundary`/`highBoundary`, keeping the attribution sentence as-is.

issues.location: 'When it does not just get slow', last paragraph: 'Sorting an already-sorted array of 200,000 integers with the naive version above confirms it on the machine used for this page: the process prints `Stack overflow.`, dumps a stack trace thousands of frames deep, and exits'
issues.problem: Every other measurement on this page is backed by a `csharp run` block and a matching (often [...]-wildcarded) output block -- this is the one claim presented as a specific, first-person-observed result ('confirms it on the machine used for this page', a quoted console line 'Stack overflow.') with no accompanying code or output block, and it could not be added the normal way since letting a StackOverflowException actually occur would crash the run-code.mjs harness itself rather than fail gracefully. The underlying fact is well documented (the StackOverflowException docs cited elsewhere on the page say exactly this), so this is not a fabrication concern, but it is the one unverifiable-by-tooling empirical claim on an otherwise fully machine-checked page.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either soften to a documentation-backed statement without the specific quoted console text and 'on the machine used for this page' framing (e.g. 'a naive version pushed this deep will terminate the process outright rather than return slowly, per the StackOverflowException documentation above'), or add a `bash run` block that shells out to a small separate program and captures/wildcards the actual crash output if the toolchain's `fails` flag can express a non-zero/aborting exit code safely.

issues.location: Opening paragraph: 'Quicksort's first-element pivot is the version most courses teach first'
issues.problem: An unsourced claim about what courses generally teach -- the mild version of the pilot-round lesson against unscoped 'what most people think'/'everybody does X' generalizations. Low-stakes (it is plausible and not load-bearing for any later claim) but exactly the shape critics were told to flag.
issues.fixLooksLike: Scope it to the algorithm rather than to courses: 'The first-element-pivot partition is the simplest version of quicksort to state' or similar, and let the rest of the paragraph do the motivating work.

note: brokenLinks/consoleErrors are the design critic's remit (verify-page.mjs); this round's AdSense review ran only run-code.mjs per its assigned checklist and left them unmeasured rather than fabricated.
